config.title: Test User Interactions

intro.title: Test User Interactions
intro.body: In this lesson, you will build a simple interactive button component and learn how to write tests for user interactions like clicks. You will use React Testing Library to simulate user events and verify that your component responds correctly. The core concept involves writing unit tests that mimic real user behavior to ensure your UI works as expected. You'll use TypeScript for type safety and Jest as the test runner. By the end, you'll be able to test user-driven changes in a React component's state or output.
intro.usecase: Testing user interactions is essential for ensuring that interactive UI components behave correctly in real applications. For example, in e-commerce checkout forms, you need to verify that quantity selectors update totals correctly and that form validation triggers appropriate error messages. In dashboard applications, you must test that filter controls properly update data visualizations and that toggle switches enable/disable features as expected. This practice prevents bugs in critical user flows like authentication modals, data table sorting, or multi-step wizards where incorrect behavior directly impacts user experience and business outcomes.

objectives: Apply React Testing Library to set up a testing environment for user interaction tests.
Use the render function to mount a React component within a test environment.
Implement screen queries to locate DOM elements for testing user interactions.
Execute userEvent methods to simulate realistic user actions like clicks and typing.
Utilize assertions with expect to verify component behavior after user interactions.
Construct test cases that simulate sequences of user interactions and verify outcomes.
Define test structures with describe and it blocks to organize interaction tests.
Invoke userEvent functions to simulate keyboard input and verify form behavior.
Handle asynchronous interactions by using findBy queries for elements that appear after state changes.
Return proper test results by using assertions that check for expected DOM changes.
Compare actual component behavior with expected outcomes after simulated user interactions.
Modify test queries to target specific elements using data-testid attributes for reliable selection.

steps.title: Import React and useState from 'react'
steps.instruction: Import React and the useState hook from the 'react' package.
steps.hint: Use the import statement to bring in React and useState from 'react'.
steps.analogousExample:
// Example of importing React and useState
import React, { useState } from 'react';
steps.seedCode: // Import React and useState from 'react' here
steps.expectedOutcome: The 'react' package is imported, making React and useState available for use in the component.
successCriteria: The code includes an import statement that imports React and useState from 'react'.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've successfully imported React and useState. This gives you access to React's core functionality and the useState hook for managing state.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but check your import syntax. Make sure you're importing both React and useState from 'react'.
steps.feedbackWrong: The import statement is missing or incorrect. You need to import React and useState from the 'react' package.

steps.title: Create the main component
steps.instruction: Create a functional component named TestUserInteractions that returns JSX. The component should be the default export.
steps.hint: You can use either a function declaration or an arrow function. Make sure to return a JSX element (like a <div>).
steps.seedCode:
import React, { useState } from 'react';

// Create the TestUserInteractions component here
steps.expectedOutcome: A functional component named TestUserInteractions is created and exported as default.
successCriteria: The component should be named TestUserInteractions, return JSX, and be exported as default.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've successfully created the TestUserInteractions component. This is the foundation for our user interaction tests.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but make sure: 1) The component is named exactly 'TestUserInteractions', 2) It returns JSX, and 3) It's exported as default.
steps.feedbackWrong: The component wasn't created correctly. Remember to create a function named TestUserInteractions that returns JSX and export it as default.

steps.title: Initialize clickCount state
steps.instruction: Inside your TestUserInteractions component, initialize a state variable called clickCount using useState. Set its initial value to 0.
steps.hint: Use the useState hook you imported earlier. Remember to specify the type as number since clickCount will be a number.
steps.analogousExample:
// Example of initializing a numeric state variable
const [clickCount, setClickCount] = useState<number>(0);
steps.seedCode:
import React, { useState } from 'react';

// Create the TestUserInteractions component here
steps.expectedOutcome: Your component will have a clickCount state variable initialized to 0, ready to track button clicks.
successCriteria: The code should include a useState call that creates a clickCount variable with initial value 0 and a setter function, with proper TypeScript typing.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've successfully initialized the clickCount state variable. This will track how many times the button is clicked.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but check that you've: 1) Used useState, 2) Named the variable 'clickCount', 3) Set initial value to 0, 4) Added proper TypeScript typing for numbers.
steps.feedbackWrong: The clickCount state wasn't initialized correctly. Make sure to use useState with an initial value of 0 and proper TypeScript typing.

steps.title: Initialize isActive state
steps.instruction: Inside your component, initialize a new state variable named 'isActive' using useState, with an initial value of false. Use TypeScript to type it as boolean.
steps.hint: Add a second useState call after your existing clickCount state. Remember to use the boolean type with useState<boolean>.
steps.analogousExample:
// Example of initializing boolean state
const [isActive, setIsActive] = useState<boolean>(false);
steps.seedCode:
import React, { useState } from 'react';

// Create the TestUserInteractions component here
steps.expectedOutcome: Your component will have two state variables: clickCount (number) and isActive (boolean).
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've successfully added a boolean state variable 'isActive' initialized to false.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but check: Did you use useState<boolean>? Is the initial value false?
steps.feedbackWrong: Try again. You need to add a second useState call for a boolean state variable named 'isActive' with initial value false.

steps.title: Define handleClick function
steps.instruction: Inside your component, define a function named handleClick that increments the clickCount state by 1.
steps.hint: Create a function that calls setClickCount with the current clickCount plus 1. You can use the previous state to calculate the new value.
steps.seedCode:
import React, { useState } from 'react';

// Create the TestUserInteractions component here
steps.expectedOutcome: You should have a handleClick function that properly updates the clickCount state when called.
successCriteria: Increments clickCount by 1 (can use previous state or current value)
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've successfully defined a handleClick function that increments the clickCount state. This function will be used later to handle button clicks.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but there might be an issue with how you're updating the state. Make sure you're calling setClickCount and properly incrementing the value by 1.
steps.feedbackWrong: The handleClick function isn't defined correctly. Remember to create a function that calls setClickCount to increment the clickCount state by 1.

steps.title: Define handleToggle function
steps.instruction: Inside your component, define a function called handleToggle that toggles the isActive state value.
steps.hint: Create a function that calls setIsActive with the opposite of the current isActive value.
steps.expectedOutcome: You should have a handleToggle function that toggles the isActive boolean state when called.
successCriteria: The handleToggle function must be defined inside the component and must toggle the isActive state value.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've successfully defined a toggle handler function that will switch the isActive state between true and false.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but make sure your function properly toggles the isActive value. Use setIsActive with the opposite of the current value.
steps.feedbackWrong: The handleToggle function isn't defined correctly. Remember to create a function that calls setIsActive to toggle the boolean state.

steps.title: Return a container div
steps.instruction: Return a div element as the main container for your component. This div will wrap all the JSX content you'll add in later steps.
steps.hint: In the return statement, replace the existing empty div with a div that will serve as your main container.
steps.expectedOutcome: Your component now returns a div element that will serve as the main container for all UI elements.
successCriteria: The component should return a JSX div element as its top-level container.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've set up the main container div. This provides the structure to add interactive elements in the next steps.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're close! Make sure you're returning a div element from your component.
steps.feedbackWrong: Let's focus on returning a div element as the container. Check that your component returns JSX with a div.

steps.title: Add a heading
steps.instruction: Inside the container div, add an h1 element with the text 'Test User Interactions'.
steps.hint:
Use JSX syntax to create a heading element:

Test User Interactions
steps.analogousExample:
// Example of adding a heading inside a container

Test User Interactions
steps.expectedOutcome: The component will have a visible heading 'Test User Interactions' at the top of its rendered output.
successCriteria: The code must include an h1 element with the exact text 'Test User Interactions' inside the container div.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've successfully added the heading to your component.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're close. Make sure you've added an h1 element with the exact text 'Test User Interactions' inside the container div.
steps.feedbackWrong: The heading wasn't added correctly. Check that you have an h1 element with the text 'Test User Interactions' inside the container div.

steps.title: Display clickCount state
steps.instruction: Add a paragraph element inside the container div that displays the current clickCount value.
steps.hint:
Use JSX curly braces to embed the clickCount state variable inside a

tag.
steps.analogousExample:
// Example of displaying a state value in JSX

Current count: {count}
steps.expectedOutcome: The component will now show the current clickCount value in a paragraph element.
successCriteria: Display the clickCount variable inside the paragraph using JSX curly braces
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've successfully added a paragraph that displays the current clickCount value. This demonstrates how to render state values directly in JSX.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but make sure you're displaying the clickCount variable inside the paragraph using curly braces like {clickCount}.
steps.feedbackWrong:
Try adding a paragraph element (

) that shows the clickCount value. Remember to use curly braces to embed the state variable in JSX.

steps.title: Add click button with onClick handler
steps.instruction: Inside the return statement of your component, add a button element with the text 'Click me' and wire its onClick event to the handleClick function.
steps.hint: Use the <button> JSX element with onClick={handleClick} and include the text content 'Click me'.
steps.analogousExample:
// Example of adding a button with onClick handler
<button onClick={handleClick}>Click me</button>
steps.expectedOutcome: A button labeled 'Click me' appears in the UI that increments clickCount when clicked.
successCriteria: onClick attribute wired to handleClick function
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've successfully added an interactive button that will trigger the click handler.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're close. Make sure you have both the button element with 'Click me' text and the onClick handler pointing to handleClick.
steps.feedbackWrong: The button isn't properly configured. Check that you have a <button> element with onClick={handleClick} and the text 'Click me'.

steps.title: Display isActive state
steps.instruction: Add a paragraph element that displays 'Active: Yes' when isActive is true and 'Active: No' when isActive is false.
steps.hint: Use a ternary operator inside JSX to conditionally render different text based on the isActive state value.
steps.analogousExample:
// Example of conditionally displaying state in JSX

{isVisible ? 'Visible: Yes' : 'Visible: No'}
steps.expectedOutcome: The UI will show whether the component is active or not based on the isActive state.
successCriteria: A paragraph element is added that uses the isActive state variable with a ternary operator to display 'Active: Yes' when true and 'Active: No' when false.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've successfully added conditional rendering to display the isActive state.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but make sure your paragraph uses the isActive state with a ternary operator to show 'Active: Yes' when true and 'Active: No' when false.
steps.feedbackWrong:
The paragraph element is missing or doesn't correctly display the isActive state. Try adding

{isActive ? 'Active: Yes' : 'Active: No'}

inside the return statement.

steps.title: Add toggle button with onClick handler
steps.instruction: Add a button element with the text 'Toggle Active' and wire its onClick prop to the handleToggle function.
steps.hint: Add a <button> element inside the container div, set its text content to 'Toggle Active', and assign the onClick prop to handleToggle.
steps.analogousExample:
// Example of adding a button with onClick handler
<button onClick={handleToggle}>Toggle Active</button>
steps.expectedOutcome: The component will have a second button labeled 'Toggle Active' that, when clicked, will toggle the isActive state between true and false.
successCriteria: The code must include a <button> element with the text 'Toggle Active' and an onClick prop set to handleToggle.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've successfully added the toggle button with the correct onClick handler. This completes the interactive component with both click counting and toggle functionality.
steps.feedbackPartial: You've added a button, but it might be missing the correct text or the onClick handler. Make sure the button says 'Toggle Active' and has onClick={handleToggle}.
steps.feedbackWrong: The toggle button is missing or incorrect. Add a <button> element with the text 'Toggle Active' and wire its onClick to the handleToggle function.
